prayer.text: Saint Augustine of Canterbury, pray for us.

cues.text: Prior of Gregory's Own Monastery
Before his mission to England, Augustine served as prior of the monastery of St. Andrew on Rome's Caelian Hill.
Pope Gregory the Great had founded it on his own family estate before his election to the papacy.
This placed Augustine among the pope's closest and most trusted monastic associates when Gregory finally set his long-deferred plan to evangelize England into motion.
A Mission Nearly Abandoned
Around June 596, Augustine set out with some forty monks on the long overland journey toward the English Channel.
Discouragement overtook the company before they had gone far, as frightening tales of the fierce, uncivilized island people they were bound to evangelize chilled their enthusiasm.
Several monks proposed turning back rather than risk the uncertain mission ahead.

Augustine, sharing something of his companions' anxiety, agreed to return in person to Rome and lay their fears plainly before Gregory himself, rather than simply overruling his brethren's genuine terror.

Gregory's response was firm but encouraging rather than harsh: he sent Augustine back to his waiting company armed with fresh letters of support, and the mission, its confidence restored, pressed on at last toward Britain.
Landing in Kent
Augustine and his companions landed on the Isle of Thanet in the kingdom of Kent in 597.
There, conditions proved more favorable than their earlier fears had led them to expect.
King Æthelberht , though himself still pagan, had married a Frankish Christian princess, Bertha .

He permitted her to bring her own chaplain and practice her faith openly at court—a quiet Christian presence already established without missionary effort through one queen's steady, patient fidelity.
Æthelberht received the missionaries cautiously but courteously, meeting them in the open air, tradition holds, out of a superstitious wariness of foreign magic.
After carefully observing their manner of life, he was himself converted and baptized, followed shortly by large numbers of his subjects.
First Archbishop of Canterbury
Before the mission reached England, Augustine had been consecrated bishop and established his episcopal seat at Canterbury , the royal capital of Kent.
There, he founded the see that has remained, for fourteen centuries since, the symbolic and historic center of the English Church.

Gregory sent Augustine the pallium — the woolen band signifying his metropolitan status and communion with the Apostolic See — along with detailed pastoral guidance on organizing the new English Church.
This included his celebrated counsel that pagan temples, rather than being destroyed outright, might often be more effectively converted to Christian use.
He also advised that familiar local customs be adapted rather than abolished wherever this could be done without compromising the faith itself.
Limits and Difficulties
Augustine's mission was not without real setbacks: an attempt to establish friendly relations and liturgical unity with the older British Christian communities ended in mutual mistrust and failure.
These communities, descendants of Roman Britain's own earlier Church, had British bishops who refused to recognize Augustine's authority or adjust their independent customs.
This created a division between the newly established Roman mission and the older native British Church that would persist for generations after Augustine's own death.
Legacy

Augustine died around 604, having lived to see the foundation of English Christianity firmly established at Canterbury, though the fuller conversion of the whole Anglo-Saxon patchwork of kingdoms would take decades more of labor by his successors.
Remembered as the Apostle of the English , Augustine remains a genuinely reassuring model for every believer nearly overwhelmed by fear before a difficult calling.
He was a missionary who came close to turning back before he had even properly begun, yet became the founder of a Church.

That enduring Church arose through nothing more dramatic than a pope's patient encouragement and his willingness to press forward despite real fear, continuing in an unbroken line from Canterbury for well over a thousand years.
